front: Describe laminar flow's velocity profile and its Doppler appearance.
back: Parabolic velocity profile (fastest at center, slowest at wall). Produces a narrow spectral envelope with a clear window.

front: Describe plug (blunt) flow. Where in the heart is it typical?
back: Flat velocity profile — all streamlines move at nearly the same speed. Typical in the LVOT and proximal aorta. Produces a narrow spectral envelope.

front: What does turbulent flow look like on spectral and color Doppler?
back: Spectral: broadening, fill-in of the envelope. Color: mosaic pattern with variance (green if variance is enabled).

front: Volumetric flow = {{c1::cross-sectional area × mean velocity}}, and stroke volume through a site = {{c2::CSA × VTI}}.

back: ΔP ≈ 4v². Peak instantaneous gradient in mmHg = 4 × (peak velocity in m/s)². Valid when proximal velocity is negligible.

front: When must the full form of the Bernoulli equation be used?
back: When the proximal velocity (v₁) is not negligible (typically > 1.5 m/s). Use ΔP = 4(v₂² − v₁²).

front: What is the continuity equation and when do you apply it?
back: At steady state, flow into a chamber equals flow out. Applied to calculate AVA from LVOT: AVA = (CSA_LVOT × VTI_LVOT) / VTI_AV.

front: What is the role of the wall filter in Doppler?
back: Removes low-frequency wall-motion artifact from the Doppler signal. Set too high, it can eliminate low-velocity flow signals of clinical interest.
